item.title: Lionesses discover Nations League opponents as Sarina Wiegman's side eye LA Olympics qualification
item.description: Sarina Wiegman 's England will face France, Austria and Portugal in the UEFA Women's Nations League, a competition that doubles as qualifying for the Los Angeles 2028 Olympics. The draw also placed the Republic of Ireland, Wales and Scotland in League A. Only the team finishing top of each group secures a place at the Games, with group winners also advancing to the Nations League semi-finals. The Republic of Ireland have the hardest-looking assignment on paper, having been drawn alongside world champions Spain, as well as Norway and Switzerland. Wales must contend with Denmark, Italy and Iceland, while Scotland's group features Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden. Northern Ireland, competing in Group B, will meet Poland, Finland and Belarus. England head coach Sarina Wiegman applauds fans after England’s Women’s World Cup qualifier against Greece (Nick Potts/PA). Matchdays one and two are set for February and March, with the third and fourth rounds of games following in April. The final league stage fixtures come in June, ahead of the Women's World Cup in Brazil. The semi-finals are due to be played in October, while the third place play-off and the final are scheduled for late November and early December. Teams finishing fourth in League A will drop into League B, while the winners of League B will move up. England missed out on the Paris Olympics in 2024 after failing to win their Nations League group the previous year. The Lionesses were placed in a group alongside the Netherlands, Scotland and Belgium. Despite winning 6-0 in their final group game against Scotland, England were still pipped to top spot by the Netherlands on goal difference. Wiegman’s team will not want to slip-up again, but will not have things all their own way in a group that also contains France. England have also not secured their spot at next year’s World Cup yet, as they must first get past Ukraine in a two-legged play-off, with the two games taking place later this month and in early December. England have achieved significant success under Wiegman in recent years, winning the Euros in 2022 and 2025, either side of making the World Cup final in 2023. They will now set their sights on qualifying for next year’s World Cup ahead of a push for Olympic glory the following year.

item.title: 10 takeaways from Oregon State’s loss at Fresno State
item.description: FRESNO, Calif. — Oregon State lost to Fresno State 38-22 Saturday night at Valley Children’s Stadium. Here are 10 takeaways as the Beavers prepare to host Texas State. 1. Reality check Two things can be true. Oregon State can still be ahead of schedule and on its way to a legitimately surprising season amid a massive rebuild, complete with a potent offense. Much of its success thus far came by pounding less talented teams and several of the worst defenses in the country. And where OSU was vulnerable was there to be exploited by teams like Fresno State, which has talent and good coaching. The Beavers are not a College Football Playoff team. That dose of reality doesn’t diminish what’s being accomplished this season. They’re simply not one of the two most talented teams in the Pac-12 right now. 2. Oregon State was outcoached JaMarcus Shephard and his staff were outcoached for definitely the first time in conference play and arguably for the first time this season. Matt Entz laid out in detail what Fresno State picked up from studying Braden Atkinson from his time at Mercer and Oregon State’s tendencies. Bye weeks also include self-scouting. Fresno State was more prepared for what OSU showed and particularly offensively the Beavers did not have an effective counter. 3. Self-inflicted errors can’t happen in games like this Winning on the road against a team with at least comparable (if not better) talent and coaching is a difficult task to begin with. It becomes a whole lot harder with six presnap penalties and allowing five sacks with two leading to fumbles. OSU absolutely could have led by multiple scores early if not for a false start negating Jake Reichle’s would-be touchdown, if Aeryn Hampton’s foot was in bounds and if multiple other penalties didn’t occur. That doesn’t even get into defensive miscues from missed tackles or over-pursuits. 4. The offensive line may have had its worst game Houston was more physically dominating than Fresno State, but that’s to be expected. Oregon State’s offensive line had a brutal showing nearly across the board, with sacks allowed by multiple players in one-on-one matchups. OSU’s rushing stats are skewed by the sacks and not nearly as poor as the final box score, but the bottom line is Fresno State won the line of scrimmage and it’s not a particularly stout group. 5. Josiah Freeman was the best receiver on the field Fresno State’s 6-foot-4 receiver had a big night with two touchdowns. Freeman had a massive advantage against Isaiah Houi and performed accordingly. If there’s one piece OSU’s receiving corps is missing it is a target with the size and length of Freeman, which the Beavers are leaning on via their tight ends. But an outside target like him is hard to beat and he showed why. 6. item.title: Eagles-Commanders Film Review: The idea that Jalen Hurts was holding this offense back should be finished by now
item.description: Aug 7, 2025; Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, USA; Philadelphia Eagles head coach Nick Sirianni talks with quarterback Tanner McKee (16) in a game against the Cincinnati Bengals at Lincoln Financial Field. Mandatory Credit: Bill Streicher-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect I’m struggling to get particularly angry about this offense anymore. There were times when watching the Eagles lose 27-10 to the Commanders bored me. We keep seeing players asked to do things that don’t suit them. Every week, I sit down hoping to see something different, and every week, it feels like I’m writing about the same problems. The Eagles scored their final points with 4:27 remaining in the first quarter. There was an awful lot of football left to sit through after that. The idea that Jalen Hurts was holding this offense back, and that everything would look dramatically different with a quarterback who preferred playing under center and throwing over the middle, should be finished by now. Tanner McKee hasn’t transformed anything. It’s the same offense, with the same limitations, and very little downfield passing game. That doesn’t mean Hurts was playing perfectly or that McKee has played well. He hasn’t. It means changing the quarterback was never going to solve all of this. The Eagles finished with 268 yards at 3.9 yards per play, and 69 of those yards came on the final possession with the game already gone. Their only touchdown followed a takeaway that gave them the ball at the Commanders’ 26-yard line. Injuries matter, obviously, but Sean Mannion and Nick Sirianni still have to put a functioning offense on the field. Right now, I don’t see the staff finding enough answers or showing much willingness to move away from what keeps failing. With that in mind, I’m going to spend more time looking closely at the younger players over the rest of the season. Their development is becoming a really important part of this year. There are still individual reps worth watching, even when the offense as a whole makes it difficult to stay interested. Let’s get into it. Offense Before this gets too miserable, let’s start with a good McKee throw! This is the sort of middle-of-the-field completion we heard about all offseason, and he deserves credit. He can make these throws. I don’t think McKee is a good player right now. His play has been pretty dull, and there is almost no vertical passing game to make watching this offense worthwhile. However, I’ve maintained all season that no quarterback would look good consistently in this situation, and I stand by that. I would absolutely expect McKee to look better in a proper scheme with protection that could handle pressure. The Eagles produced +0.30 EPA per pass play from a clean pocket in this game and -0.95 under pressure. You still have to evaluate the quarterback, but you can’t ignore the conditions around him. item.title: Report: OKC Thunder add Dalen Terry to 15th NBA roster spot
item.description: The Oklahoma City Thunder have filled their final roster standard spot. They have reportedly signed Dalen Terry to a two-year deal, per ESPN's Shams Charania. After a little bit of an adventure with the No. 15 spot, they finally land on a guy. Terry has played the last four seasons in the NBA. He was the No. 18 pick of the 2022 NBA draft. He spent the first three-plus years with the Chicago Bulls before finishing last season with the Philadelphia 76ers . The 24-year-old has averaged 3.5 points on 44.3% shooting, 1.7 rebounds and 1.2 assists in his career. After the Thunder lost Chet Holmgren, Jalen Williams and Cason Wallace for the foreseeable future — and maybe for the entire 2026-27 season for the latter two — they had to fill in the vacant roster spot. Leaving it open was a luxury they couldn't afford any longer. As mentioned earlier, it's been quite the ride to get to this point. The Thunder had previously signed Ochai Agbaji to a standard roster spot deal this past Friday. And then OKC backed out of it on Saturday. They had to recalibrate after learning Holmgren will miss two-plus months with a torn patellar tendon. Now, Terry joins the Thunder. Shai Gilgeous-Alexander led them to a much-needed win over the Cleveland Cavaliers on Monday. But they still badly need NBA-capable bodies to fill out their rotation. The hope is that he can be one of those guys. G/F Dalen Terry has agreed on a two-year deal with the Oklahoma City Thunder, sources tell ESPN. Terry enters his fifth NBA season after the former No. overall 18 pick spent time in Chicago and Philadelphia, and went to training camp with Golden State last month. pic.twitter.com/JlVzvyRcC4 — Shams Charania (@ShamsCharania) November 3, 2026 This article originally appeared on OKC Thunder Wire: Report: OKC Thunder add Dalen Terry to 15th NBA roster spot

item.description: Pacers forced to play with just six players after lengthy injury report originally appeared on The Sporting News . Add The Sporting News as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Many NBA teams can say that they're short-handed early in the 2026-27 season. Jalen Williams and Chet Holmgren are out for the Thunder , Anthony Edwards is missing time for the Timberwolves , and Ja Morant is dealing with an injury for the Trail Blazers . But nothing can compare to the situation the Pacers endured on Monday night. Between longer-term absences and late scratches, Indiana had just six players available to play against the Hawks . A few rather inexperienced NBA players were forced to play over 40 minutes for the Pacers, who still kept it close in a 108-104 loss despite being so short-handed. Here's a look at Indiana's lengthy injury report from Monday's game. Pacers injury report vs. Hawks The following players were out for the Pacers on Monday night: Tyrese Haliburton (hamstring) Pascal Siakam (rest) Johnny Furphy (knee) T.J. McConnell (hamstring) Larry Nance Jr. (illness) Andrew Nembhard (cervical) Aaron Nesmith (hamstring) Ben Sheppard (knee) Obi Toppin (lumbar sprain) Ivica Zubac (ankle) Kelly Oubre Jr. (knee) That left just six players available for head coach Rick Carlisle to even play: Jay Huff, Quenton Jackson, Jarace Walker, Braden Smith, Kobe Brown and Jalen Slawson. Of that bunch, Smith, Brown and Slawson are all on two-way deals. The last time a team used six or fewer players this early in an NBA season was in 1948, when the Lakers used just five in their third game of the season, according to ESPN. It also marked the first time since 2004 that the Pacers used just six players in a game — that instance was the day following the "Malice at the Palace" between Indiana and Detroit that led to multiple suspensions. "People are still talking about that game," Carlisle said postgame about that 2004 game, per ESPN . "And they will talk about this game for a long time." The chaos surrounding eligibility dragged through the summer and into the fall, leaving teams with roster uncertainty right up to the start of the season. After so many months of off-the-court headlines, though, the focus of college basketball is finally right back where it belongs: on the hardwood. item.title: Why Alexander Zverev’s rise to world No 1 rings hollow
item.description: This Monday, when the ATP tennis rankings were updated, there was a new name at the top of the list. Alexander Zverev has capped the best year of his life by ascending to world No 1 for the first time, at the conclusion of a season in which the 29-year-old finally ended his grand slam drought with two titles. It has been an excellent year for one of tennis’s most consistent athletes, who has been a fixture in and around the top 10 since 2017. On paper, the German’s story is one of triumph over adversity, of the extraordinary difficulty of managing type 1 diabetes with life as an elite athlete and not letting health conditions inhibit one’s sporting dreams. He overcame a debilitating ankle injury sustained in the French Open semi-finals in 2022, which left him needing to be helped off court in a wheelchair. Then there are the infamous slam finals, the total and utter implosions from two-sets-to-love up and two-sets-to-one up against Dominic Thiem and Carlos Alcaraz respectively at the US Open 2020 and Roland-Garros 2024. He overcame that psychological turmoil too , finally breaking his duck at the French Open this year. But Zverev’s ascent to the top of the sport in many ways feels hard to celebrate. The feelgood story summarised above, of resilience and discipline, is all true. Yet, if true, other stories about his history and character may make it ring hollow to many observers uncomfortable with his continued presence in the sport at all. He has been accused by two former partners of domestic abuse , allegations which Zverev adamantly denies. Olga Sharypova made allegations of physical and emotional abuse against him in interviews with Racquet magazine in 2020 and Slate in 2021, but did not bring a court action, insisting she only wanted to share her story and to inspire women in similar situations to come forward. Zverev settled out of court with another ex-partner , Brenda Patea, in 2024, after he had previously been issued a penalty order – which occurs under German law where the evidence for one side is considered compelling and a trial deemed unnecessary – and fined. The court was clear in its statement after the 2024 settlement: “The decision is not a verdict and it is not a decision about guilt or innocence.” Zverev has since inaccurately claimed it proved his innocence. He has not been convicted. There has been no verdict at all, leaving him in a limbo state, a grey space with no legally definitive outcome but where the harrowing details of the accusations cannot be forgotten by those who have read them. He is obviously not the first sportsman to be in this position, nor will he be the last. That does not detract from the severity of what he has been accused of and the inability of many tennis viewers to, in good conscience, support him. item.title: ‘Somebody’s going to get the blame’: Von Miller points the finger elsewhere after Cowboys loss
item.description: Mandatory Credit: Troy Taormina-Imagn Images On Sunday, the Dallas Cowboys fell to the Arizona Cardinals, leaving fans utterly shocked by the unraveling. The overtime thriller ended with a Cardinals field goal to seal the 33-30 win, and another loss for the Cowboys’ disappointing season. For the fifth consecutive time, the Cardinals have defeated the Cowboys on their home turf, marking a 5-0 record at AT&T Stadium. The latest loss has led to a lot of criticism for the coaching staff, especially head coach Brian Schottenheimer. But after the game, veteran linebacker Von Miller came to their defense a bit. The Comeback Down 30-24, Cardinals quarterback Gardner Minshew rallied the team late in the fourth quarter, ultimately finding wide receiver Michael Wilson in the back of the end zone with seconds left on the clock. Cardinals kicker Chad Ryland lined up for a normal extra point but missed left, leaving the score tied and Cowboys fans relieved. To start overtime, both teams failed to find field goal range until the Cardinals put their second and final possession to use. After a Wilson 17-yard catch and a Tyler Allegier run for 11 yards, Ryland found a comfortable position for redemption and sealed a 33-30 victory. Dallas led by two touchdowns early in the fourth quarter but crumbled in the last 16 minutes of regulation. Veterans Speak Up Nothing new for longtime Cowboys players and fans, especially linebacker Von Miller, but after the loss, the 16-year veteran gave a balanced response, defending the coaching staff for any blame that may come as a result. “I’m a parent,” Miller said, via Jon Machota of The Athletic . “I got three kids. Sometimes you raise your kids a certain way, and you teach them lessons. You expect them to act a certain way when they go out. “And sometimes the kids just go out there and do things that are not a reflection of who you are as a parent. And I use that reference for our coaching staff. We have amazing coaches that keep us prepared, ready to go mentally, physically, emotionally. They breathe life into us, and just for whatever reason, that’s the product. “The product that went out there is not a reflection of our coaching staff. This is pro sports. This is not parenting. So at the end of the day, the buck has to stop somewhere. Somebody’s going to get the blame. “But my opinion, this is just me, I don’t know nothing about football. I only played 16 years. We’ve got great coaches. We’ve got a great coaching staff. And that’s not a reflection of how they coach us and get us ready every week.” Despite the apt analogy, Miller failed to realize that paid athletes, like in any professional field, have expectations, and if not met, repercussions follow. The Cowboys haven’t had a Super Bowl season since 1996, and most sports enthusiasts point the finger at owner Jerry Jones. With a 3-5 record, the Cowboys aren’t out of the race, as the NFC East is still up for grabs. It will be interesting to see who the finger is pointed at

item.description: Police in Spain have confirmed they have opened a “routine” investigation into possible involuntary manslaughter following the death of Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel, who died in hospital on Tuesday after suffering a cardiac arrest as a result of a collision during a match on Monday. De Miguel, 30, collapsed on the pitch after a clash with Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono, who had rushed out of his area to clear the ball but struck the forward in the chest. The match was then abandoned and Owono was shown a red card following the incident, which took place in stoppage time of the second division fixture. De Miguel was taken to hospital after receiving treatment on the pitch. Tenerife initially reported that he was “stable, despite the severity of his condition” before reporting that his neurological condition had worsened in the early hours of Tuesday. They confirmed his death at around 8am on Tuesday. Under Spanish law, any death that is deemed non-natural automatically triggers a judicial inquiry. In a statement, Tenerife said: “Heartbroken, with a lump in our throats and unable to believe this is true, we at CD Tenerife announce the tragic passing of Jesus de Miguel Alameda. There are no words of comfort. There is absolutely nothing that can ease this overwhelming sense of sadness.” Owono, a Equatorial Guinea international, has deactivated his Instagram account since the incident. McDaniel described the Dodgers and Mets as the primary bidders in his free-agent rankings , while placing the Yankees among the teams thinking about Skubal. The distinction matters. Considering a run is not the same as making an offer, and no agreement or specific Yankees trade has been reported in McDaniel’s assessment. Punchoutpitch shared the report Tuesday. Mandatory Credit: Michael McLoone-Imagn Images Credit: IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect What Skubal would give the Yankees Skubal posted a 2.72 ERA with 186 strikeouts over 158 2/3 innings in 2026 between Detroit and Los Angeles. He won the American League Cy Young Award in both 2024 and 2025 before the Tigers traded him to the Dodgers at the 2026 deadline. At his best, the left-hander is the type of pitcher who can change a postseason series. Pairing him with Cam Schlittler and Max Fried would give New York a formidable top of the rotation, with Gerrit Cole and Carlos Rodon also part of the current pitching picture. The cost would be enormous. McDaniel projects an eight-year, $352 million contract, a forecast rather than a reported asking price or offer. item.title: Points Galore: What the Prem’s High-Scoring Start Means for Totals and Try-Scorer Betting
item.description: The Prem has never started a season quite like this. The opening weekend produced 52 tries, the most for any first round in the league’s history, and a fortnight later Saints and Bath shared 18 of them in a 71-48 shoot-out at Franklin’s Gardens. Then Round 4 came along, and five matches produced about 160 points between them, roughly half the rate of the first three weekends. So which is the real Prem? Is this now a league where you simply back the over, or did September fool everyone? With Christian Wade one try away from holding the competition’s all-time try-scoring record outright, it’s a good moment to look at what the numbers mean for the two markets most affected: total points and try-scorers. A September like no other Round 1’s 52 tries beat every previous opening weekend, and Round 2 added 41 more, giving an average of 9.3 tries a match across the first two rounds, the highest in Opta’s records. By the end of Round 3 the league had seen 142 tries in 15 matches, about 9.5 a game, and 949 points, or roughly 63 a match. The headline acts were easy to spot. Saints’ 71-48 win over Bath brought 119 points, the second-highest total in league history, behind only their own 94-33 demolition of Bristol in May. Gloucester put 48 past Quins without reply, Bristol beat Saints 41-26, and Sarries edged Tigers 40-38 at Welford Road. None of this came out of nowhere, though. The try count has gone up every season for four years: Season Tries per match 2022/23 7.01 2023/24 7.06 2024/25 7.96 2025/26 8.60 2026/27 (first two rounds) 9.30 Why the tries keep coming The laws have helped. Recent tweaks around kicking mean players in front of the kicker can no longer loiter offside, scrum-halves get more protection at the base of the ruck, and shot clocks have cut the dead time. Saints boss Phil Dowson put it simply: “There have been some rule changes from a kicking point of view that’s opened the game up.” He added that “risk is being rewarded more often and there’s the actual skill level of the playing group.” The bonus point matters too. The Prem still awards one for four tries, whatever the opposition scores, while the Top 14, Super Rugby and the Champions Cup ask for a three-try margin. A side chasing its fourth try in the last ten minutes, even with the result settled, is good news for anyone holding an over. Then there’s the lack of jeopardy at the bottom. There’s no automatic relegation this season, which takes some of the fear out of a struggling side’s game plan. Add firm pitches and a dry ball in September, and the attack had every advantage. Not everyone is convinced it’s progress. The Telegraph’s Charles Richardson argued: “Tries are only worth as much as the strength of the defence trying to prevent them.” Round 4 suggested the defences haven’t given up just yet.
